images.text:
I've been thinking a lot about inequality and injustice. Someone recently asked me who a personal hero of mine was. I guess I should have thought a little longer, but I immediately answered, Martin Luther King, Jr. I ought to have added that not only is he a hero, but also an inspiration. If you don't know about Martin Luther King, Jr., you can find lots of information about him on the Internet.

Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. was born in 1929 in Atlanta, Georgia, in the United States. Even though black people ought to have had equal rights during that time, they did not. Black Americans were obligated to move to the back of buses so white people could sit in the front or stand when there were no seats for white people. Separate restrooms and drinking fountains, as well as segregated schools, were everywhere. As citizens and people who fought for their country, the lives of black Americans should have been far better.

Martin Luther King, Jr., a minister in a Baptist church, wanted equal rights for all people, so he began the fight against racial segregation. However, he did not condone using violence in this fight. He believed that if you use violence to express yourself, you will cause more violence. He encouraged people to fight peacefully, with civil disobedience, asking black people to sit in the front instead of the back of the bus. In Washington D.C., over 200,000 people came to listen to his speech asking the U.S. government to change laws against its black citizens. There were many discriminatory laws that should have changed sooner. Thanks to Martin Luther King, Jr., civil laws began changing in the United States.

However, there were a large number of white people who disagreed with him and his beliefs. If people fear change and unfamiliar situations, they may react in an extreme way. This was especially evident when, sadly, Martin Luther King, Jr. was assassinated by a white man in 1968.

On the third Monday of January each year, Americans honor Martin Luther King, Jr. They think about how Martin Luther King helped in the fight for equality. They also realize that America should continue to change to improve the lives of many who are still not seen as equals to this day. If we remember Martin Luther King, Jr.'s vision and bravery, we will work toward a more peaceful future for all people.

Should Have, Ought to Have for Obligation and Recommendation
When you want to talk about something that didn't happen in the past and that you are sorry that it didn't happen, you can use should have or ought to have.
You use should have/ought to have + past participle to indicate some regret or criticism about past actions, events or situations and to talk about obligations that were unfulfilled.

For example:
We should have waited for the snow to stop. (I'm sorry we didn't.)
I ought to have been more sensitive about the matter. (I regret that I wasn't.)
You shouldn't have been so hasty in your decision. (Criticism.)
They should have called to let you know they weren't coming. (Past obligation.)
I guess I should have thought a little longer.
I ought to have added that not only is he a hero, but also an inspiration.
Even though black people ought to have had equal rights during that time, they did not.
Black people's lives should have been better.
There were many discriminatory laws that should have changed sooner.
You use the First Conditional to talk about events or situations that are likely to happen.
To be precise about the certainty or nature of the event taking place, you can choose to use a variety of modal verbs such as:

will (99% certain)
If we invite Joe, he'll be really happy.

can (ability)
If I go too, I can give you a ride.

going to (intention)
If I see her, I'm going to give her a big hug.

must (necessity)
If you go on a vacation, you must have a valid passport.
